strengths: The paper addresses an identifiable audience in program analysis and code representation learning. Transferring information from source code and descriptions into lower-level representations is a useful research question.
The architecture is understandable at a high level: frozen source/comment representations guide a trainable encoder, followed by contrastive learning with interpolated representations.

The evaluation covers four downstream tasks and reports promising improvements against the listed baselines, including function-name accuracy of 33.41 versus 29.41 for RoBERTa and summarization BLEU-4 of 34.36 versus 32.43 for GraphCodeBERT.
The manuscript includes component ablations, a CodeT5 extension, qualitative examples, and a public code/data archive reference. These provide useful foundations for further investigation and reuse.
weaknesses: Necessary—resolve the evaluation protocol. Section 2.3 describes supervised functionality classification with cross-entropy, but Section 3.2 and Table 2 specify non-overlapping POJ-104 problem labels across training, validation, and testing. The manuscript does not explain how unseen labels are predicted; Figure 10 instead resembles retrieval. Specify the actual task, training objective, prediction procedure, and definitions of MAP/MAR/MAF1. This ambiguity affects the main results and central ablations. Also reconcile Section 3.2's validation-set evaluation for AnghaBench with Section 4.3's test-set description.

Necessary—align the binary-code claims with the evidence. The experiments use LLVM IR compiled from available source code, and Figures 7–8 retain informative function, global, and structure names. This does not establish performance on stripped executables. The footnote asserting that these representations are trivially interchangeable is inaccurate. Document compiler settings and identifier handling, and either narrow the claims to source-generated LLVM IR or provide representative evidence using stripped binaries and their lifted representations.

Necessary—control the attribution to interpolation and staged learning. PCL and the no-interpolation ablation receive 10 pre-training epochs, whereas the full model receives 30 or 70. The assertion that PCL converges does not establish a comparable training control. A comparison using the same data and update budget is needed to distinguish the proposed components from additional domain adaptation. Separate scalar and feature-wise interpolation if retaining claims about their individual contributions, and report uncertainty for the smaller gains.

Necessary—qualify the human-versus-synthetic comment conclusion. Table 7 reports a collapse from 38.19 to 3.06 MAF1 with human comments, but Section 5.2 does not adequately specify comment extraction, function alignment, coverage, or controlled comparisons on the same functions. Length distributions do not establish the proposed causal explanations involving verbosity and implementation detail. Moreover, removing generated comments decreases MAF1 by only 0.79 points. Diagnose and replicate the collapse, or restrict the conclusion to the particular preprocessing and training configuration tested.

Necessary—support or narrow the semantic-comprehension claims. BLEU, GLEU, ROUGE, and exact match measure textual agreement; they do not establish functional equivalence of generated code or faithful summaries. No systematic human evaluation is reported despite RQ2 invoking human perception. Clarify the provenance and quality of summarization references, and provide semantic validation appropriate to the claims, such as assessed summaries and compilation/execution checks. Alternatively, describe these results as improvements in reference-text matching. Selected positive examples cannot establish general semantic consistency or long-range comprehension.

Necessary—correct consequential presentation inconsistencies. Figure 3 feeds concatenated embeddings to the interpolation network, whereas Equations 8 and 10 use their sum. The implementation and gradient treatment of the model-dependent targets should be specified consistently. Section 5.1 also reports MAF1 decreases of 2.07, 7.46, and 18.25 points, whereas Table 7 gives 0.79, 2.85, and 6.97 points; the prose appears to confuse relative percentages with point differences. These issues impede reproduction and interpretation.

Optional—condense the repeated human-learning analogies and strengthen the embedding discussion with quantitative neighborhood measurements in the original embedding space. These would improve clarity and insight, but the recommendation primarily reflects unresolved evidence and protocol concerns.
